query: For the equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy and its equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets that are single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain why their mechanical properties differ during deformation and failure when constituent count alone is inadequate? Specify a controlled comparison, predictions relative to the quinary baseline, the applicable boundary conditions, supporting evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Differences in mechanical properties among equiatomic FCC Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni-based alloys arise because composition-dependent local lattice distortions (as indicated by MSAD) create varying dislocation glide-resistance landscapes. In particular, higher Cr content increases MSAD and thus raises the extrapolated 0 K CRSS (solid-solution strengthening), while increased Mn and Fe content fosters dynamic solute pinning (Portevin–Le Chatelier effect) at elevated temperatures via elastic solute–dislocation interactions.
generation.material_initial_state: Homogenized, water-quenched, equiatomic FCC single crystals of quinary, quaternary, and ternary Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni-derived alloys, oriented in the [1̄23] direction and prepared by Bridgman or optical floating-zone methods, then annealed as specified.
generation.intervention: Compression experiments over a temperature range (9–1373 K) combined with strain-rate jump tests, TEM analysis of dislocation structures, and DFT calculations to quantify MSAD and assess dislocation glide resistance across the different compositions.
generation.conditions: Single-crystal compression at an engineering strain rate of 1×10⁻⁴ s⁻¹, with additional strain-rate jumps (1×10⁻⁴ to 1×10⁻² s⁻¹) during low-hardening Stage I deformation (~10% plastic strain). Measurements focus on temperature regimes outside the inertial (<60–77 K) and high-temperature diffusion-active (above ~673 K) ranges where distinct mechanisms (inertial motion and PL effects) become operative.
generation.structural_mediator: The local lattice distortions quantified by mean-square atomic displacement (MSAD), which vary with composition (especially Cr content), mediating the resistance to dislocation glide.
generation.mechanism: At cryogenic temperatures, reduced phonon drag allows thermally activated dislocation glide to be strongly affected by solid-solution obstacles modulated by local lattice distortions. At higher temperatures (≈673–873 K and beyond), diffusible Mn- and Fe-rich solutes form atmospheres that elastically pin dislocations (via a Cottrell-type mechanism), leading to serrated flow (Portevin–Le Chatelier effect).
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the quinary baseline, quaternary and ternary alloys that contain less Cr (and thus lower average MSAD) will exhibit a lower extrapolated 0 K CRSS and a smaller increase in CRSS due to the PL effect at high temperatures. Conversely, alloys with relatively higher Mn and Fe content are predicted to show a more pronounced PL strengthening increment.
generation.baseline: Room-temperature CRSS data and thermal activation model extrapolations (without low-temperature inertial effects) from quinary Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloys (and previously studied CrFeCoNi and CrCoNi single crystals) serve as benchmarks for comparison.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to equiatomic FCC single-phase Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni-based concentrated solid solutions evaluated as [1̄23]-oriented bulk single crystals in compression; it is valid in temperature regimes below inertial-dominated (<60–77 K) and above the onset of dynamic solute pinning (≈673 K), with the established processing (annealing, quenching) conditions.
generation.uncertainty: While MSAD is expected to correlate with extrapolated 0 K CRSS, uncertainties remain regarding the precise role of potential Suzuki segregation effects in some compositions (e.g., CrFeNi) and the quantification of the solute–dislocation interaction strength compared to lattice distortions.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform systematic temperature-dependent compression tests on comparable quinary, quaternary, and ternary single crystals to obtain CRSS from 0.2% offset yield stresses and confirm slip systems via slip-trace identification. Use strain-rate jump tests to identify transitions into inertial and PL regimes. Conduct TEM analyses to assess dislocation core structures and measure partial-dislocation dissociation widths at room temperature and high temperature (e.g., 1173 K). Compare the extrapolated 0 K CRSS against DFT-derived MSAD values across compositions.
measurements: CRSS vs. temperature curves from cryogenic (<77 K) to high temperatures (up to 1373 K).
Strain-rate sensitivity and activation volume from strain-rate jump testing.
Stress–strain curves to detect serrated flow indicative of the PL effect.
TEM measurements of dislocation dissociation widths and stacking-fault energies.
DFT calculations of MSAD correlated with the extrapolated lattice resistance (τ₀/μ).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the quaternary and ternary alloys do not show systematically lower extrapolated 0 K CRSS and diminished PL-related CRSS increments as predicted from their reduced MSAD compared to the quinary baseline, or if TEM data reveal solute segregation mechanisms (e.g., Suzuki-type) that contradict the expected dominant role of lattice distortion and Cottrell pinning, then the hypothesis will be rejected.
